newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Dollar seen vulnerable vs yen in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Dollar seen vulnerable vs yen in 1997.

text.p: While the U.S. dollar might brush past its 1996 highs against the yen early next year, foreign exchange forecasters expect the U.S. currency to fall below its current level over six- and 12-month time horizons.

AT 1300 EST/1800 gmt on Tuesday, dollar/yen was trading at slightly above 113. Analysts said they saw room for it to retest the 115 yen area in the new year before it starts a decline to 106 yen by year end.

"In the first quarter you're going to see the same forces as we've seen of late, which is a significant move towards dollar strength, then capped basically at 115 by the perception the central banks don't want it to go above there," said Alan Ruskin, research director at I.D.E.A. Inc.
The average forecast of 10 U.S. economists surveyed by Reuters placed dollar/yen at 109.70 by June 1997, with a gradual depreciation to 106.00 expected by next year's close.
By mid-year, renewed trade frictions between the U.S. and Japan should start to cast a shadow on dollar/yen, while a possible Bank of Japan tightening may bolster the yen, they said.

Ruskin, who's projections of 110 yen in six months and 105 yen in 12 months, were closest to the survey's consensus forecasts, said the recent slowdown in this year's narrowing of Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. will reassert itself as 1997 progresses.
"That is going to be the primary factor, rather than any tightening," he added.
Chase Manhattan Bank had the rosiest six-month outlook with dollar/yen rising to 116 yen, while First Chicago NBD Bank held the most bullish one-year forecast, also of 116.
Chris Widness, international economist at Chase said he sees Japan's trade surplus still "tending to decline" during the first half of 1997, allowing the dollar some scope to appreciate.

But as Japan's trade surplus starts to widen again later in the year, the dollar should start falling towards Chase's 110 yen year-end target before Japan's exporters have a chance to respond fully to the yen's slide this year, Widness said.
The gloomiest outlooks came from Smith Barney, forecasting 98 yen per dollar in six-months' time and Norwest Corporation's forecast for a dollar/yen rate of 99 in one year's time.
Norwest Corporation chief economist Sung Won Sohn said the yen was currently grossly undervalued based on purchasing power parity models.

Economists expect Japanese interest rates to increase next year, with one forecasting the Bank of Japan will raise Japan's official discount rate at least one percent from its current record low of 0.5 percent, where it has stood since September 1995.

"The BOJ has created too much liquidity trying to hold the value of the yen down," Sohn said. "They are going to be concerned about inflation so they will start mopping up some excess liquidity as a result of stronger economic growth."
But not all analysts interviewed said that a Japanese credit tightening would necessarily deflect the dollar from its path higher.

Even if Japan pushed short-term rates up 75 or 100 basis points, Japan would still have some of the lowest interest rates among major nations, giving investors little incentive to keep funds parked in yen instruments.
Higher Japanese rates might initially jolt the market as yen-financed leveraged carry trades get reversed, but it should not change investment flows that much, experts said.

"There will be a sudden shock, then we'll go back to Japan exporting lots and lots of capital every quarter," said Kevin Harris, international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch who declined to participate in the formal survey.

But even with dollar/yen hovering less than one-and-a-half percent below the 42-month high of 114.92 set in late-October and yield-starved Japanese investors still prowling for fatter returns, analysts said the dollar may not be able to muscle to another major new high in the short-term.
"You could see another spike up because of outflows from Japan, but I don't think we're going through 115 (dollar/yen)," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at Bank of Montreal in Chicago.
